questions.question: What does polymorphism mean in C++?
questions.explanation: Polymorphism allows the same name to be used for different purposes, i.e., one name, many forms.

questions.question: Which of the following is a type of polymorphism in C++?
questions.explanation: C++ supports both compile-time (static) and runtime (dynamic) polymorphism.

questions.question: Compile-time polymorphism is also known as:
questions.explanation: Compile-time polymorphism is also called static or early binding.

questions.question: Runtime polymorphism is also known as:
questions.explanation: Runtime polymorphism is also called dynamic polymorphism or late binding.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of compile-time polymorphism?
questions.explanation: Function overloading is resolved at compile time.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of runtime polymorphism?
questions.explanation: Virtual functions enable runtime polymorphism.

questions.question: Function overloading is resolved at:
questions.explanation: The compiler decides which overloaded function to call based on arguments.

questions.question: Virtual functions are resolved at:
questions.explanation: Virtual function calls are resolved at runtime using the vtable.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to declare a virtual function?
questions.explanation: The virtual keyword is used in the base class to enable runtime polymorphism.

questions.question: What is function overriding?
options: Defining multiple functions with the same name
Redefining a base class function in the derived class with the same signature
questions.explanation: Function overriding provides a new implementation for a base class virtual function in the derived class.

questions.question: Which of the following is necessary for runtime polymorphism?
questions.explanation: Runtime polymorphism requires inheritance and virtual functions.

questions.question: What is a pure virtual function?
options: A virtual function with a definition
A virtual function with no definition, declared as = 0
questions.explanation: A pure virtual function is declared with = 0 and makes the class abstract.

questions.question: What is an abstract class?
options: A class with only static members
A class that contains at least one pure virtual function
A class that cannot be inherited
questions.explanation: An abstract class has at least one pure virtual function and cannot be instantiated.

questions.question: Can an abstract class be instantiated?
questions.explanation: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated directly.

questions.question: What is a virtual destructor?
options: A destructor that deletes virtual functions
A destructor declared with the virtual keyword
A destructor that is pure virtual
A destructor that cannot be overloaded
questions.explanation: A virtual destructor ensures that the correct destructor is called when deleting a derived object via a base pointer.

questions.question: Why is a virtual destructor needed?
options: To properly destroy derived class objects through base class pointers
questions.explanation: Without a virtual destructor, deleting a derived object via a base pointer may cause undefined behavior.
Due to virtual function, the derived class version is called, so output is Derived.

questions.question: What is the output if the virtual keyword is removed from the base class show()?
questions.explanation: Without virtual, the function call is resolved at compile time based on the pointer type, so Base is called.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a type of polymorphism?
questions.explanation: Sequential is not a type of polymorphism.

questions.question: Operator overloading is an example of:
questions.explanation: Operator overloading is resolved at compile time.

questions.question: Function overriding is an example of:
questions.explanation: Function overriding with virtual functions is runtime polymorphism.

questions.question: What is the vtable in C++?
options: A table of virtual function pointers
questions.explanation: The vtable is used to resolve virtual function calls at runtime.

questions.question: Which of the following can be virtual?
questions.explanation: Only member functions can be virtual. Constructors cannot be virtual.

questions.question: Can a constructor be virtual?
questions.explanation: Constructors cannot be virtual because the object's type is not fully determined until construction is complete.

questions.question: Can a destructor be virtual?
questions.explanation: Destructors can and should be virtual in base classes with virtual functions.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about pure virtual functions?
options: They have no body and are declared with = 0
questions.explanation: Pure virtual functions have no implementation in the base class and are declared with = 0.

questions.question: What happens if a derived class does not override a pure virtual function?
options: The base class function is called
The derived class also becomes abstract
The derived class can be instantiated
questions.explanation: If a derived class does not implement all pure virtual functions, it remains abstract.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of polymorphism?
options: It allows code to be written generically and reused
It removes the need for inheritance
questions.explanation: Polymorphism allows writing generic code that can work with objects of different types.

questions.question: Which of the following demonstrates polymorphism?
options: A base class pointer pointing to derived class objects
questions.explanation: Using a base class pointer to call virtual functions on derived objects is a classic example.
Without virtual, the function is called based on the pointer type, so A is printed.

questions.explanation: With virtual, the derived class version is called, so B is printed.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about virtual functions?
questions.explanation: Virtual functions are the mechanism for runtime polymorphism.

questions.question: What is late binding?
options: Function call resolved at load time
Function call resolved at compile time
Function call resolved at link time
questions.explanation: Late binding means the function call is resolved at runtime, which is done via virtual functions.

questions.question: What is early binding?
options: Function call resolved at compile time
Function call resolved at link time
Function call resolved at load time
questions.explanation: Early binding means the function call is resolved at compile time, as in function overloading.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a valid use of polymorphism?
options: Using a base class pointer to call derived class methods
questions.explanation: Global variables are not related to polymorphism.

questions.question: Which of the following is a compile-time polymorphism technique?
questions.explanation: Templates are resolved at compile time, so they are compile-time polymorphism.
ptr points to a Derived object and print() is virtual, so Derived is printed.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about virtual functions and constructors?
options: Constructors cannot be virtual, but destructors can be
questions.explanation: Constructors cannot be virtual; destructors can and often should be virtual.

questions.question: What is the main difference between function overloading and function overriding?
options: Overloading is runtime, overriding is compile-time
Overloading is compile-time, overriding is runtime
questions.explanation: Overloading is resolved at compile time; overriding is resolved at runtime with virtual functions.

questions.question: Which of the following allows a class to be polymorphic?
questions.explanation: Virtual functions make a class polymorphic by enabling runtime binding.
